excluded.name: Popobawa
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Unverified, one source. Living belief tied to real fear, assault and politics; the most feared attacks are sexual. Not suited to a game enemy; listed so the owner sees it. | license red: First reports are from 1965 (Pemba), peak 1995: modern origin, folklore age unverified.

excluded.name: Buda
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Unverified, one source. RED: the belief is aimed at real groups (blacksmiths, Beta Israel) and fuels stigma. Never use the name. A generic hyena-man should carry no Ethiopian label.

excluded.name: Mamlambo
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Unverified, one source. The page calls her a goddess of rivers; living belief with real deaths attached. Listed so the owner sees it. | license red: First dated record is 1997 news: modern origin, folklore age unverified.

excluded.name: Inkanyamba
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Unverified, one source. RED: the page calls it a deity and says it must be appeased. Do not use as an enemy.

excluded.name: Apep
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Unverified, one source. RED: a god of chaos, a deity.

excluded.name: Mushussu
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Unverified, one source. RED: sacred beast of a god (Marduk), though that religion is extinct.

excluded.name: Namahage
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: A living New Year ritual, considered a visiting toshigami deity; not an enemy. Listed for the owner only. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Akkorokamui
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Name includes kamuy (god) and the Ainu are a living culture; the page marks claims of reverence as disputed. Treat as not an enemy until the owner decides. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Xingtian
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Described as a deity and a symbol of defiance; not an enemy. Listed for the owner only. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Gonggong
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: A deity (a malevolent water god); never an enemy. Listed for the owner only.

excluded.name: Cailleach
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Treated as a deity of weather and land; never an enemy. Listed so the owner sees it. unverified, one source

excluded.name: Domovoy
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Household guardian linked to ancestors in living belief; never an enemy. Listed for the owner.

excluded.name: Taniwha
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red as an enemy: many iwi regard taniwha as kaitiaki (guardians), and taniwha have shaped modern road and court decisions. The same source shows dangerous stories exist, but Te Ara returned HTTP 403, so I cannot show an iwi-sanctioned monster use. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Te Wheke-a-Muturangi
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red until the owner decides: it is tied to named ancestors (Kupe, or Tamatea in another iwi's version), so it is an ancestor story with competing iwi versions. Te Ara not readable. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Rainbow Serpent
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red: a creator being worshipped in ritual across many nations. Listed so the owner sees it; do not use. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Moo
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red: revered as aumakua (family guardians), and named moo guard places. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Tzitzimitl
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red: celestial female deities tied to fertility and childbirth; post-conquest writers called them demons. Fits a cracked sky but must not be used. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Cipactli
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red: first day-sign of the sacred count and, in some versions, the earth deity. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Pishtaco
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red: scholars read it as a symbol of colonial exploitation, and belief in it caused real killings in 1983 and 1988. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Trauco
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red: the lore has been used to excuse sexual violence, so I advise against it. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Wendigo
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red: belief of living peoples; the source notes a scholar objecting to outsider horror use. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Skinwalker
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: Red: Navajo people are reluctant to share it with outsiders, and a Cherokee scholar says outsiders should not discuss it. Unverified, one source.

excluded.name: Mae Nak
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A real shrine where devotees pray for easy childbirth and leave offerings today; she is treated as a revered figure, not just a monster.

excluded.name: Phi Ya Nang
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A protective boat spirit honored by southern Buddhist fishermen and the Royal Thai Navy today. Not an enemy.

excluded.name: Kapre
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. The page says the name and image grew from colonial prejudice against dark-skinned Aeta/Negrito people, so a design risks reading as a stereotype of a real ethnic group. Recommend skipping or a heavy redesign; owner dec

excluded.name: Bakunawa
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. It figured in babaylan rituals and merged with naga and Rahu; some retellings call it a goddess turned serpent. Communities still make noise at eclipses.

excluded.name: Rangda
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Her mask is kept in a village death temple and used in sacred dance; a ritual figure, not an enemy.

excluded.name: Orang Minyak
excluded.origin: Malay urban legend; Malaysia and Singapore
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Most versions make him a sexual predator; not suitable. | license red: Modern origin: first record is a 1957 Singapore newspaper report and a 1958 film, so a modern invention.

excluded.name: Sanni Yakku
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A living Sinhalese healing ritual still performed on the south coast; using the masks would borrow a sacred performance. Owner decides.

excluded.name: Naga
excluded.origin: Hindu, Buddhist, Thai, Khmer and Javanese tradition
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. Revered: Thailand made the naga a national symbol in 2022, and many Khmer see themselves as naga descendants. Never an enemy.

excluded.name: Garuda
excluded.origin: Hindu and Buddhist tradition; India, Thailand, Indonesia
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A sacred mount and the national emblem of Thailand and Indonesia. Not usable as an enemy.

excluded.name: Makara
excluded.reason: sensitivity red: unverified, one source (Wikipedia only); second source to be checked before art. A sacred vehicle and temple guardian; most stone taps in Nepal are still carved as makara.
